text: A golden path, also called a paved road, is the first concrete thing a platform run as a product actually ships: an opinionated, supported, well-documented default way to build and deploy a service. This lesson is about why that specific combination matters, and why unlimited freedom to build it any way you like isn't actually the generous option it sounds like once more than one team is involved.

Opinionated means it makes real decisions instead of handing you a menu. Supported means the platform team maintains it and answers for it when it breaks, instead of it being a script someone wrote once and abandoned. Documented well enough means a team can follow it without a Slack thread just to get started. Put those together and you get the property that actually matters: easy to follow, because it's genuinely the path of least resistance, and hard to misuse, because the guardrails are built in, not optional.

Unlimited freedom sounds generous, but at the scale this course assumes — many teams, shared security and compliance obligations — it doesn't produce ten good, independently-optimal decisions. It produces ten snowflake systems, each needing its own mental model and its own security review, because none of them can be assumed to work like any other. The organization pays for that in onboarding time, in incident response, and in the platform team's own ability to improve anything at all.

That's why the distinction between a golden path and a mandate matters. A golden path stays the easiest option, but a team isn't technically blocked from deviating for a real reason — they just give up the support the platform was carrying for free: their own security review, their own on-call for anything the platform would have handled automatically. That asymmetry, supported by default and on your own if you leave, is what keeps most teams on the path without anyone forbidding the alternative outright.

Good golden paths are rarely invented from a blank page — they're almost always a pattern that already worked well for one strong team, generalized so everyone else can reuse it, which is also why baking security and compliance into the template pays off: a service built on it inherits those controls automatically. Next, this chapter asks the harder question — once a golden path exists, how do you actually know if it, and the platform around it, is helping?
